# Periplasmic Chaperones: Outer Membrane Biogenesis and Envelope Stress

**Authors:** Ashton N. Combs; Thomas J. Silhavy

**Affiliations:** Department of Molecular Biology, Princeton University, Princeton, New Jersey, USA

## Abstract

Envelope biogenesis and homeostasis in gram-negative bacteria are exceptionally intricate processes that require a multitude of periplasmic chaperones to ensure cellular survival. Remarkably, these chaperones perform diverse yet specialized functions entirely in the absence of external energy such as ATP, and as such have evolved sophisticated mechanisms by which their activities are regulated. In this article, we provide an overview of the predominant periplasmic chaperones that enable efficient outer membrane biogenesis and envelope homeostasis in Escherichia coli. We also discuss stress responses that act to combat unfolded protein stress within the cell envelope, highlighting the periplasmic chaperones involved and the mechanisms by which envelope homeostasis is restored.

## INTRODUCTION

Gram-negative bacteria such as Escherichia coli possess a characteristic, multilayered cell envelope that is marked by the presence of two membranes: a cytoplasmic, or inner, membrane and an outer membrane (OM). A thin peptidoglycan cell wall is contained within the aqueous cellular compartment delineated by these two membranes, a distinct subcellular space first termed the periplasm in 1961 by Peter Mitchell (110). Biochemical studies conducted around that time suggested that several degradative enzymes, such as alkaline phosphatase and ribonuclease, were confined within a discrete extracytoplasmic compartment in a manner analogous to mammalian lysosomes (53, 94, 95), thus alluding to one of the primary functional advantages of cellular compartmentalization. Beyond containing the cell wall and serving to sequester degradative enzymes, the periplasm houses a multitude of proteins involved in various critical cellular processes, including periplasmic binding proteins that are involved in nutrient transport, chemotaxis, and quorum sensing; chaperones and proteases involved in cell envelope homeostasis; and components of each of the cellular machineries required for building the OM (49, 149).

It has long been appreciated that the OM of gram-negative bacteria functions as a robust permeability barrier that excludes large and hydrophobic molecules from the cell while still permitting the uptake of small-molecule nutrients (117). This selective permeability of the OM endows gram-negative bacteria with an innate resistance to many antibiotics and represents a major obstacle for antibiotic discovery in the modern era (85). Furthermore, mounting evidence suggests that the OM imparts considerable mechanical strength to the cell envelope and thereby compensates for the thin peptidoglycan cell wall to maintain cellular mechanical integrity (160). The OM contains four major components—lipopolysaccharide (LPS), phospholipids, lipoproteins, and β-barrel outer membrane proteins (OMPs)—and is a uniquely asymmetric lipid bilayer. While the inner membrane is a traditional phospholipid bilayer, OM lipids are asymmetrically distributed, with phospholipids located in the inner leaflet and LPS located in the outer leaflet. It appears that we now know all of the components of each of the basic cellular machineries required to build the OM: the LPS transport (Lpt) complex for LPS; the AsmA-like proteins YhdP, TamB, and YdbH for phospholipids; the localization of lipoprotein (Lol) pathway for lipoproteins; and the β-barrel assembly machine (Bam) complex for OMPs (for a review of OM biogenesis, see 49).

OMPs are collectively present in hundreds of thousands of copies per cell (87) and perform a number of diverse functions critical to cell viability, including nutrient uptake (117), toxin efflux (88), protein secretion (44), and adhesion (90). Only two OMPs are essential in E. coli (15, 177), and they are those that are required to build the OM itself: LptD, which inserts LPS into the OM as part of the Lpt complex (13, 178), and BamA, the central component of the Bam complex that catalyzes the assembly of OMPs into the OM (169, 177). OMPs, like all OM constituents, are synthesized in the cytoplasm and thus must first be secreted across the inner membrane. Most proteins that localize to the cell envelope or beyond, including OMPs, are secreted from the cytoplasm by the general secretory (Sec) system (25, 36), and as such enter the periplasm in a linear, unfolded form starting from the N terminus. Following their translocation across the inner membrane, OMPs, aided by molecular chaperones, must then diffuse across the aqueous periplasmic space in an unfolded yet folding-competent state before being assembled into the OM (Figure 1). This cellular feat is particularly challenging because the periplasm lacks any obvious energy source, such as ATP. It has long been known that many ATP-dependent molecular chaperones utilize ATP binding and hydrolysis to regulate their affinity for substrates and catalytic activity (70). As all periplasmic chaperones are by default ATP independent, diverse and sophisticated mechanisms by which the activity of periplasmic chaperones is regulated have emerged (112). Still, all proteins in the extensive network of periplasmic chaperones and proteases share the fundamental function of assisting proteins toward their native folds and/or minimizing the accumulation of misfolded states, states that, if left unchecked, can often lead to toxicity or even lethality.

Accordingly, several stress responses function in part to combat protein stress within the envelope and maintain cellular homeostasis. Although both the sources of envelope stress and activating signals that elicit a cellular response vary, the envelope stress responses that respond to protein stress generally act to restore protein homeostasis through the upregulation of proteases to promote unfolded protein degradation and/or the upregulation of molecular chaperones to facilitate protein folding. These responses must be both swift in onset and appropriately controlled to ensure cellular survival and avoid inadvertent toxicity, the need for which is perhaps best exemplified by the σE stress response in monitoring unfolded OMP accumulation in the periplasm (see “Envelope Stress Responses” below). Indeed, unfolded OMPs are exceptionally toxic (74), and the cell goes to great lengths to ensure constant monitoring and regulation of OMP synthesis, responding promptly to periplasmic stress to ultimately avoid lethality. Moreover, full constitutive activation of the σE stress response causes OM permeability defects and stationary-phase lysis, underscoring the need for its proper control (for a review of envelope stress responses, see 109).

Here, we provide an overview of the predominant periplasmic chaperones that together act to ensure efficient OMP biogenesis and maintain envelope homeostasis in gram-negative bacteria. We limit our discussion to what is known about E. coli—for which the periplasmic chaperone network has been most extensively characterized—but note that variations on these paradigms are known to exist for other gram-negative organisms. We focus on the molecular chaperones and proteases for which the most functional information is known within the context of OMP biogenesis. We also discuss protein-folding catalysts—disulfide oxidoreductases and peptidyl-prolyl isomerases (PPIases)—as well as the stress-specific chaperones that respond to acid and bile stress. Lastly, we provide a brief overview of each of the envelope stress responses that collectively act to combat unfolded protein stress in the periplasm.

## PERIPLASMIC CHAPERONES AND PROTEASES

### SurA

surA was initially identified in a screen for genes that were essential for survival in stationary phase (sur) (167), and later characterization of surA null mutants demonstrated its clear role in OMP biogenesis (82, 105, 137). Numerous genetic, biochemical, and proteomic studies support the notion that SurA functions as the primary periplasmic chaperone in E. coli and facilitates transport of the bulk mass of OMP substrates to the OM (34, 136, 150, 168). Loss of SurA produces evident defects in OM biogenesis, indicated by an increased sensitivity to detergents and antibiotics, induction of the σE envelope stress response, and a reduction in OM density (82, 105, 137, 150). The OM defects of a surA null mutant are compounded by the fact that the β-barrel component of the Lpt machinery, LptD, is heavily reliant on SurA for its proper assembly in E. coli (168).

Structurally, SurA contains three distinct domains: a core domain formed from its N- and C-terminal regions and two parvulin-like PPIase domains, P1 and P2 (10) (Figure 2a). The SurA core domain alone is responsible for the majority of chaperone activity, as a variant lacking both PPIase domains retains chaperone activity in vitro and nearly completely complements a surA null mutant in vivo (8). However, the contributions of the PPIase domains to the conformational dynamics and chaperone activity of SurA become appreciable when OMP biogenesis is compromised through mutations in bamA or bamB (134, 153).

SurA preferentially binds to peptide sequences of high aromatic content with affinities in the low micromolar range (11, 12). SurA–OMP binding occurs between specific segments along unfolded OMP substrates and a groove formed between the core and P1 domains of SurA (20, 96), with more than one SurA molecule capable of interacting with a single substrate at once (20, 86, 96, 144, 164). Substrate binding causes both conformational changes in SurA (20) and a dynamic expansion of the unbound regions of the OMP substrate (22, 86, 96), which may help maintain unfolded OMPs in a folding-competent state and/or enable efficient downstream recognition by the OM assembly machinery. Subsequent substrate delivery to the OM is facilitated by a direct interaction between SurA and the Bam complex (9, 145, 150).

### Skp

The periplasmic chaperone Skp (seventeen kilodalton protein) has a long and colorful history. Initially characterized as a DNA-binding protein (54, 55), subsequent research indicated that Skp is, in fact, localized to the periplasm and likely binds unfolded OMP substrates directly (165, 166). This speculation was confirmed by the demonstration that Skp binds to several different OMPs in vitro (23), including newly translocated, unfolded substrates (142). Despite these early implications of a role in OMP biogenesis, the precise functions of Skp remain an active area of investigation.

Deletion of skp has no significant effect on OM density or abundance of OMPs in the OM (34, 150). However, depletion of SurA in a skp null strain has a profound effect on the OM proteome, resulting in a decreased OM abundance of nearly every β-barrel OMP (34), and ultimately causes synthetic lethality (136, 150). These observations, along with the fact that depletion of SurA alone significantly reduces OM density (150), are consistent with a primary role for SurA in OMP biogenesis, whereby the chaperone activity of Skp becomes critical only under conditions of periplasmic stress, such as that of a surA null.

Skp exists structurally as a trimer with a jellyfish-like architecture that consists of a β-barrel core and three long α-helical tentacles (75, 172) (Figure 2b). Each Skp monomer contributes three β-strands to form a nine-stranded, discontinuous β-barrel trimerization core, while each tentacle comprises two long α-helices arranged in a hairpin extension that is reminiscent of a coiled coil. The cavity formed by the three tentacles of the Skp trimer serves as the substrate binding site for OMPs (18, 171), and the flexibility of the tentacle arms allows expansion of the binding cavity to accommodate substrates of various sizes (56, 143). Additionally, multiple Skp trimers can bind a single substrate at once to accommodate larger OMPs that cannot be fully sequestered by a single expanded Skp binding cavity (143, 164).

Skp binds substrates with a high affinity and remarkable stability, displaying global dissociation constants in the low nanomolar range (114, 119, 126) and complex lifetimes that exist on the order of hours (18). Skp–OMP complex binding comprises multiple weak, transient interactions of a sequence unspecific nature that together enable high-affinity, long-lived binding through avidity (18, 125, 126). Substrates bound within the Skp cavity undergo rapid structural interconversion and expansion (18, 22), which, when coupled with the weak local affinity of Skp for any particular polypeptide segment, could feasibly facilitate substrate release through both recognition of the β-signal by downstream assembly machinery and the subsequent thermodynamic stability provided by OMP folding and integration into a membrane environment (18, 114). Indeed, incubation of Skp–OMP complexes with BamA-containing proteoliposomes allows for productive substrate release and assembly (121, 144). Moreover, Skp can facilitate the direct insertion of OMPs into negatively charged phospholipid bilayers in vitro (17, 120), as well as the inner membrane in vivo (45), in a BamA-independent manner.

At physiological concentrations, Skp exists in an equilibrium between monomeric and trimeric states (140). Monomeric Skp is intrinsically disordered, is functionally inactive, and undergoes a coupled disorder-to-order transition and trimerization in response to substrate binding (97). Importantly, this activation mechanism provides a means by which the high-affinity binding and chaperone functions of Skp, which could represent a potential hazard to the cell if left uncontrolled, can be carefully controlled in response to periplasmic stress through shifting of the Skp monomer–trimer equilibrium. Additionally, strong regulation of Skp activity might explain how the chaperone activity of SurA could predominate under nonstress conditions despite a weaker affinity for unfolded OMP substrates (144, 164).

Consistent with a more critical role in quality control during OMP biogenesis, Skp functions to remove β-barrel OMPs that fail to assemble in a timely manner from the Bam complex and directly facilitates their degradation by the periplasmic protease DegP (see “DegP” below) (24). Substrate OMPs that have initiated folding but have not yet membrane integrated are subject to sequestration and removal from the Bam complex by Skp, thus imposing a quality control mechanism that ensures the rapid membrane integration of β-barrel OMPs. Following substrate displacement from the OM assembly machinery, Skp directly mediates OMP degradation by serving as a sacrificial adaptor protein for DegP; both Skp and its bound substrate undergo concerted proteolysis as a consequence of the high stability of the Skp–OMP complex. These quality control functions, along with the observation that surA and skp deletions differentially affect the assembly of OMPs harboring mutations in the β-signal (173), reflect the stringent requirement for both proper substrate recognition and assembly by the Bam complex in the chaperone activity of Skp.

### DegP

degP was first identified through its role in degrading mutant periplasmic proteins (156) and its requirement for survival at high temperatures (91, 157). DegP is a serine endoprotease that exhibits general protease activity against a wide variety of unfolded substrates, including mutant periplasmic and hybrid proteins (156, 157), mislocalized cytoplasmic proteins (151), nonnative and unfolded substrates (73, 92), misfolded pilin subunits (59, 62), and unfolded periplasmic proteins and OMPs (104, 154). Reflective of a central role in cell envelope homeostasis, expression of degP is upregulated by both the σE and Cpx envelope stress responses (see “Envelope Stress Responses” below) (32, 38). Moreover, degP null mutants exhibit a number of synthetic phenotypes with other known protein-folding factors and proteases involved in cell envelope biogenesis and homeostasis (136, 150, 175).

The DegP monomer is structurally defined by three distinct domains: a trypsin-like serine protease domain and two PDZ domains, PDZ1 and PDZ2 (Figure 2c). The basic structural unit of DegP is a trimer, which in the absence of substrate can form a proteolytically inactive hexamer through staggered association of two trimeric rings (76). Upon substrate binding, DegP trimers and hexamers become proteolytically active and assemble into large, cagelike polyhedron structures containing 12, 18, 24, or 30 subunits (61, 66, 78) that are stabilized through PDZ1–PDZ2 interactions between neighboring trimers (61, 66, 67, 159) and remain assembled until the substrate is depleted (66). While DegP cage assembly is not required for proteolysis or survival at high temperatures (67), it likely serves as an additional mechanism by which proteolysis is regulated, as mutations that both stabilize the active conformation of DegP and prevent cage assembly confer dominant lethality at high temperatures due to rogue protease activity (68).

Cleavage of unfolded or nonnative substrates by the protease domain is rather indiscriminate, with a preference for cleaving substrates after Ile, Val, Thr, Ala, and, to a lesser extent, Met, Ser, and Leu (73, 77). Cleavage specificity is also influenced by the PDZ1 domain, which acts to tether the substrate to DegP through binding of C-terminal substrate residues (60, 77). Binding of linked substrate degrons by the protease and PDZ1 domains promotes allosteric activation, driving cage assembly and proteolysis (66). As the PDZ1 and protease domains have similar substrate specificities (77), peptide cleavage at the protease domain often creates a product that is subsequently capable of binding the PDZ1 domain for further rounds of proteolysis. Additionally, several native periplasmic proteins enhance DegP activity or substrate specificity. YjfN has been reported to function as a suicide activator that activates DegP during its degradation and promotes DegP-mediated proteolysis of other misfolded substrates in trans (69). Furthermore, both CpxP and Skp function as sacrificial adaptor proteins to enhance DegP substrate specificity for misfolded pilin subunits and assembly-compromised OMPs, respectively; in either case, the chaperone is degraded alongside its bound substrate by DegP (24, 59).

DegP has also been reported to have chaperone activity that is independent of its proteolytic activity (154), although its contribution to OMP biogenesis appears to be rather minor. Use of low temperatures or the proteolytically inactive active-site mutant DegPS210A promotes refolding of MalS and citrate synthase in vitro (154). Moreover, overexpression of DegPS210A can, to some extent, suppress the temperature sensitivity of both degP and surA degP null mutant strains (136, 154) as well as the lethality caused by expression of assembly-defective OMPs in a degP null mutant background (21, 103). However, as even DegPS210A cages assume a proteolytically active conformation in the substrate-bound state (66, 78), unfolded OMPs bound by wild-type DegP would be highly likely to undergo proteolysis in vivo. Additionally, because DegP proteolytic activity rapidly increases in a nonlinear fashion at temperatures above 30°C (154), the proteolytic activity of DegP would predominate both at physiological temperatures and under heat shock conditions.

### FkpA

The periplasmic protein FkpA (FK506-binding protein A) has long been known to be involved in OMP biogenesis (105), be regulated by the σE stress response (31), and possess both chaperone and PPIase activity for nonnative or mutant proteins (3, 14, 132). However, the mechanism by which FkpA serves as a chaperone for OMPs and the physiological conditions under which it does so remained largely obscure for many years. Disruption of fkpA only slightly increases OM permeability and modestly induces σE activity (105), indicating that the contribution of FkpA chaperone activity to OMP biogenesis is relatively minor under nonstress conditions. Rather, FkpA activity appears to be more critical under conditions of periplasmic stress, particularly those of heat shock (3, 42).

FkpA exists structurally as a homodimer, with each monomer comprising two distinct domains: an N-terminal domain of three α-helices that interlace with those of the other monomer to facilitate dimerization and a C-terminal domain that is homologous to FK506-binding proteins and contains the catalytic PPIase activity (3, 141) (Figure 2d). The FkpA dimer assumes a V shape, in which each C-terminal domain is connected to its N-terminal dimerization domain through a long and flexible α-helix that may allow the FkpA dimer to adapt to different substrates (141).

FkpA binds to and increases the folding yield of several different substrate OMPs in vitro (35). Notably, this observed chaperone activity of FkpA is marked by a decrease in OMP folding rate and is distinct from the chaperone activities of either SurA or Skp. FkpA–OMP binding and chaperone activity are exerted through an extensive interaction interface that spans the inner surfaces of the N- and C-terminal domains, both of which are required for tight binding and chaperone function (35).

Additionally, FkpA shares a redundant function with Skp in the assembly of LptD that is notably distinct from that of SurA (146). FkpA is also essential for both HK97 phage infection and the lytic activity of imported colicin M (27, 58).

### BepA

BepA (β-barrel assembly–enhancing protease A) is a periplasmic, M48 family zinc metalloproteinase that possesses both chaperone and protease activities important for the proper assembly of LptD (116). An early indication of σE-dependent regulation (133) and chemical profiling of bepA null mutants (118, 161) first implicated BepA in OMP biogenesis, and a later study demonstrated that the OM permeability phenotypes observed upon bepA disruption are attributable primarily to defects in LptD assembly (116).

BepA comprises two structural domains: an N-terminal protease domain and a C-terminal tetratricopeptide repeat (TPR) domain (29, 147) that facilitates the interaction of BepA with both LptD and the Bam complex (29, 116) (Figure 2e). In addition to the TPR domain, the β2 edge strand of the BepA protease domain directly interacts with LptD during its assembly on the Bam complex, an interaction that is critical for both the chaperone and proteolytic activities of BepA (113). Through these interactions, BepA both promotes proper LptD assembly by the Bam complex—likely through facilitating the association of LptD with LptE (113, 116)—and degrades LptD substrates that fail to complete folding (113, 116, 152). While both DegP and the M48 metalloproteinase YcaL act to degrade assembly-compromised LptD at early stages in OMP assembly (84, 152), BepA is capable of degrading LptD substrates that have stalled much later in the assembly process (152). The protease activity of BepA is regulated through a reversible autoinhibitory mechanism mediated by the zinc ligand residue His-246 present in the loop region containing the α9-helix; mutational alteration of His-246 zinc coordination through either the bepAH246A mutation or deletion of the α9/H246 loop increases BepA protease activity, while tethering of the α9/H246 loop through intramolecular disulfide bonds represses it (30).

### Spy

Spy (spheroplast protein y) is a largely stress-specific periplasmic chaperone that was first identified through its readily detectable abundance in spheroplasts but not intact cells (50). Later studies demonstrated that Spy expression is regulated by both the Cpx and Bae envelope stress responses (128, 130) and strongly induced by protein denaturants such as butanol (16), ethanol (19), and tannins (181), thus implicating Spy in envelope biogenesis and/or homeostasis. The chaperone activity of Spy was first realized though a genetic selection for mutants that stabilized expression of an unstable variant of immunity protein 7 (127). Isolated mutants greatly overproduced Spy, which, when purified, reduced aggregation and enhanced refolding of a number of substrate proteins in vitro, suggesting general chaperone activity.

Spy exists as a dimer in solution, with each monomer consisting of four α-helices that adopt a hairpin-like conformation (79, 127) (Figure 2f). The Spy dimer assumes a cradle-like shape containing a concave surface of highly positive charge that directly interacts with the substrate (51, 57, 72, 127). Notably, Spy binds the unfolded, intermediate, and native states of immunity protein 7 with comparable affinities and facilitates protein folding while still bound to the substrate, a process that is dependent on weak interactions and is substrate specific (111, 158, 176). Long-range electrostatic interactions allow Spy to rapidly bind unfolded substrates, while subsequent short-range hydrophobic interactions act to stabilize the formed complex and facilitate substrate release following the hydrophobic collapse of the client protein upon folding (72). These interactions allow the substrate to sample multiple conformations across its folding landscape while still being protected from aggregation (57).

In the context of OMP biogenesis, massive overproduction (>1,000-fold) of Spy can rescue the LptD assembly defects of a Δskp ΔfkpA double-deletion strain but not a ΔsurA strain (146). Moreover, Spy binds to and reduces the aggregation of certain OMPs in vitro by maintaining them in a predominantly unfolded state, in a manner that may allow some secondary structure to form (52).

## PROTEIN-FOLDING CATALYSTS

### Disulfide Oxidoreductases and Isomerases

For many bacteria, disulfide bonds are important for the folding and stability of numerous proteins that localize to the cell envelope and beyond. The prototypical E. coli disulfide bond formation (Dsb) system is contained within the cell envelope and consists primarily of the periplasmic disulfide oxidoreductase DsbA, which catalyzes substrate oxidation (7), and the inner membrane protein DsbB, which reoxidizes DsbA that has become reduced through its oxidation of substrate (6), thereby allowing a new catalytic cycle to begin. The Dsb system in E. coli additionally contains the periplasmic disulfide isomerase DsbC and the inner membrane protein DsbD, which act to rearrange nonnative disulfide bonds and ensure that proteins adopt correct, native ones; DsbC catalyzes disulfide rearrangement through reduction and isomerization of the substrate (106, 135, 148), while DsbD serves to maintain DsbC in a reduced state such that catalysis can reoccur (108, 135, 155; for a review, see 81).

The Dsb system is essential for anaerobic growth in E. coli (80, 101, 102, 138) and is particularly critical for the proper folding of two essential substrates, the cell division protein FtsN (102) and LptD (138); thus, proper disulfide bond formation is crucial for both cell division and OM biogenesis. Folding of both FtsN and LptD is heavily dependent on the catalytic activity of DsbA, as dsbA null mutants produce substantially lower amounts of correctly folded protein, especially during anaerobic growth (101, 102, 138). In the absence of external oxidation provided by either an aerobic environment or chemical oxidants, the significantly reduced levels of functional FtsN or LptD, or both, are likely limiting for the growth of dsbA null mutants under anaerobic conditions. While these observations suggest that the catalytic activity of DsbC does not significantly contribute to the folding of either protein under endogenous conditions, particular defects of a dsbA null strain can be partially complemented by monomeric DsbC mutants that allow DsbC to be reoxidized by DsbB (4, 101) or through DsbC overexpression (106).

### Peptidyl-Prolyl Isomerases

It has long been known that the cis–trans isomerization of proline residues is often an important— and frequently rate-limiting—step in protein folding. PPIases are a widespread superfamily of protein folding catalysts that allow the normally slow process of proline cis–trans isomerization to occur on a biologically relevant timescale. The PPIases were first discovered in porcine kidney extracts and comprise the cyclophilin, FK506-binding protein, and parvulin protein families, termed as such after the drugs for which they are targets (cyclosporin and FK506) or the homology they bear to the E. coli cytoplasmic PPIase parvulin (37). E. coli contains four PPIase homologs that exert their activities in the periplasm. In addition to the abovementioned FK506-binding protein FkpA and the parvulin-like protein SurA, E. coli contains a cyclophilin homolog, PpiA, and a second parvulin-like protein, PpiD. Notably, strains carrying null mutations in all four PPIases are viable, exhibiting only a slightly decreased growth rate and increased OM permeability (63).

Little is known, however, about the specific physiological roles of PpiA and PpiD in the context of envelope protein folding and homeostasis. While ppiA expression is known to be regulated by the Cpx stress response (123), ppiA null mutants display no apparent phenotypes in either growth or the folding of periplasmic and OM proteins (71). Similarly, and contrary to initial reports (33), studies have demonstrated that disruption of ppiD has no significant effect on OMP biogenesis or OM permeability (63, 98) and the parvulin-like domain of PpiD appears to be devoid of PPIase activity (174). Purified PpiD can prevent the aggregation of citrate synthase in vitro in a manner that is independent of its parvulin-like domain, and PpiD overexpression can partially restore growth of a surA skp strain (98). While biochemical and proteomic studies suggest that PpiD may interact with the topologically similar inner membrane protein YfgM and the Sec translocon (93, 139), how either PpiA or PpiD functions in vivo within the context of OMP biogenesis and the periplasmic chaperone network remains largely unclear.

### Stress-Specific Chaperones

Enteric bacteria must survive various hostile conditions within the gastrointestinal tract of warm-blooded organisms that normally act as barriers to other bacteria, including gastric acid in the stomach and bile in the duodenum, in order to successfully colonize the lower intestine. Acid stress, like bile stress (26), is acutely deleterious due to its tendency to induce widespread protein unfolding and subsequent aggregation. Accordingly, E. coli contains a number of stress-specific chaperones that act to protect periplasmic proteins from the detrimental effects of these protein-unfolding agents.

As the OM allows free diffusion of small and hydrophilic molecules of less than roughly 600 Da, the periplasm is readily vulnerable to changes in external pH. E. coli contains two small periplasmic chaperones, HdeA and HdeB (Figure 1), that undergo chaperone activation in response to acidic pH and protect periplasmic proteins from acid-induced aggregation (41, 65). Notably, HdeA is a conditionally disordered, ATP-independent chaperone that undergoes activation by unfolding; upon exposure to low pH, well-folded, chaperone-inactive HdeA dimers undergo dissociation and partial unfolding, producing partially disordered, chaperone-active HdeA monomers that stably bind unfolded substrates to prevent their aggregation (40, 41, 162, 163). Following pH neutralization, HdeA facilitates the slow release of substrates in a manner that likely serves to minimize the concentration of aggregation-prone intermediates, thereby allowing substrates to productively refold (162). Intriguingly, both HdeA and HdeB have been reported to bind and suppress the pH-induced aggregation of a broad range of substrates including both SurA and DegP (179, 180), suggesting that HdeA and HdeB protect other periplasmic chaperones and proteases during acid stress to ensure their functionality upon return to neutral pH. While HdeA exhibits robust chaperone activity at pH 2 (28, 41, 65), the chaperone activity of HdeB is instead optimal at pH 4, a pH at which HdeB remains dimeric and is largely folded (28). These distinct activation mechanisms and chaperone activities thereby allow HdeA and HdeB to provide protection from acute acid stress over a broad pH in a manner that is regulated at the posttranslational level, thus affording a response that is orders of magnitude faster than either transcriptional or translational control.

To combat periplasmic protein aggregation induced by bile, E. coli expresses the periplasmic, glycerol-3-phosphate-binding chaperone UgpB (Figure 1). UgpB prevents bile-induced aggregation of a number of different substrates in vitro under conditions in which UgpB appears to be uniquely capable as opposed to other known periplasmic chaperones, including SurA, Spy, and OsmY (83). Importantly, UgpB exhibits chaperone activity only in the glycerol-3-phosphate-free state, a state that is assumed following the transition to low pH and subsequent neutralization. Thus, the chaperone activity of UgpB is regulated by ligand binding and dissociation in a manner that would allow UgpB to be chaperone active in the bile-rich duodenum following its transit through the acidic stomach.

## ENVELOPE STRESS RESPONSES

Three envelope stress responses in particular function in part to combat unfolded protein stress within the cell envelope of E. coli, namely the σE, Cpx, and Bae responses. Here, we provide a brief overview of the various sources of envelope stress and sensing mechanisms that elicit a cellular response, highlighting the periplasmic chaperones involved and the mechanisms by which envelope homeostasis is restored.

### σE

The σE stress response principally monitors unfolded OMP accumulation in the periplasm (100), as well as the accumulation of off-pathway intermediates in LPS biogenesis (89). Under noninducing conditions, σE is sequestered at the inner membrane by the anti-sigma factor RseA (107, 122), which undergoes regulated intramembrane proteolysis in response to the accumulation of unfolded OMPs in the periplasm (1, 2, 47, 64, 170). Sequential cleavage of RseA by the inner membrane proteases DegS and RseP (1, 2, 64, 170) allows the release of a small, soluble fragment of RseA bound to σE into the cytoplasm, and the subsequent degradation of the RseA fragment by cytoplasmic proteases facilitates σE release and downstream expression of the σE regulon (2, 39, 64; for additional review, see 5, 109).

Induction of the σE regulon elicits a multifaceted cellular response that collectively acts to reduce the burden of unfolded OMPs in the periplasm through one of three general means: increasing the efficiency of OMP assembly by upregulating the expression of folding factors, decreasing OMP synthesis by downregulating OMP translation, or increasing unfolded OMP degradation by upregulating the expression of periplasmic proteases. The efficiency and capacity of OMP assembly are increased through the upregulated expression of Bam complex subunits as well as several molecular chaperones, including SurA, Skp, FkpA, and BepA (133). Moreover, two small noncoding RNAs, MicA and RybB, act to repress translation of the most abundant OMPs—OmpF, OmpC, and OmpA—thereby reducing substrate flux through the OMP biogenesis pathway (43). Lastly, σE induction upregulates the expression of periplasmic proteases that act to degrade unfolded OMPs, most notably DegP (133). Together, these responses effectively act to reduce unfolded OMP stress in the periplasm and maintain envelope homeostasis.

### Cpx

The Cpx stress response has long been thought to chiefly respond to perturbations at the inner membrane. While the Cpx stress response is known to be induced by a plethora of signals (129), the principal commonality among these inducing signals is the generation of misfolded inner membrane or periplasmic proteins. Additional noteworthy signals that induce Cpx activity include elevated pH, high osmolarity, peptidoglycan defects, alterations in membrane phospholipid content, and defects in lipoprotein trafficking (46, 99, 129). Signal transduction following the sensing of inducing cues is accomplished via a canonical two-component system comprising the CpxA sensor histidine kinase and the CpxR response regulator (for additional review, see 46, 129).

Cpx activation results in the upregulated expression of several periplasmic factors including chaperones, folding catalysts, and a protease, which collectively facilitate the refolding or degradation of misfolded proteins. The periplasmic protein CpxP is one of the most highly induced members of the Cpx regulon (124) and serves to inhibit Cpx activation, endowing the system with a mechanism of feedback inhibition (131). CpxP also exhibits weak chaperone activity that is notably important for combating the toxicity of misfolded pilin subunits in the periplasm, directing the degradation of both CpxP and its bound substrate by DegP (59). Other noteworthy regulon members include the chaperone Spy, the folding catalysts DsbA and PpiA, and the protease DegP. Cpx activation also acts to negatively regulate Skp expression through a small noncoding RNA—CpxQ—that is derived from the transcript of cpxP, likely to prevent the lethal, Skp-mediated insertion of OMPs into the inner membrane (45).

### Bae

The Bae stress response, like the Cpx response, senses and responds to envelope stress (128) via a canonical two-component system comprising the BaeS sensor histidine kinase and the BaeR response regulator. While the Bae response can be activated by a variety of toxic molecules, including indole (128) and ethanol (19), among several others (19, 48, 109), it appears to comprise a relatively small regulon. Notable Bae regulon members include the periplasmic chaperone Spy (19, 128) and the MdtABC-TolC efflux pump (19, 115), both of which are upregulated upon Bae activation. The upregulation of these two principal regulon members could therefore help ameliorate unfolded protein stress and reduce the intracellular concentration of toxic molecules, thereby enabling cellular survival during envelope stress.

## CONCLUSION

More than six decades of investigation have led to our current understanding of the gram-negative periplasm. Envelope biogenesis and homeostasis are exceptionally elaborate processes and as such require a multitude of specialized periplasmic chaperones to ensure cellular survival in the complex and often hostile environments that gram-negative organisms inhabit. Remarkably, these chaperones function entirely in the absence of exogenous energy such as ATP and have evolved diverse and sophisticated mechanisms by which they regulate their activity, including oligomer assembly and disassembly, disorder-to-order and order-to-disorder transitions, ligand binding, and even constitutive chaperone activity that utilizes substrate folding to drive client release.

A clear functional understanding of the predominant periplasmic chaperones in E. coli has emerged; numerous lines of evidence support the notion that SurA serves a primary role in OMP biogenesis, whereas the joint activities of Skp and DegP—while capable of supporting productive OMP assembly—are far more critical for proper protein quality control. The necessity of these three principal periplasmic chaperones for efficient envelope biogenesis and homeostasis is underscored by their marked upregulation by the σE response under conditions of envelope stress, upon which their activities become crucial for cellular survival. Beyond the detailed characterizations of these three principal periplasmic chaperones, we now have an extensive understanding of the chaperones that facilitate disulfide bond formation and respond to acid stress, and the capacity for bile-responsive chaperones to combat unfolded protein stress in the periplasm is beginning to be realized.

Comparatively little is known, however, about the periplasmic PPIases as a whole, and the physiological conditions under which their activities become strictly necessary remain to be determined. Moreover, and above all, far less is known about how the activities of many periplasmic chaperones are integrated and cooperatively function within the cell envelope. Intricate in vivo studies dissecting the collective specificities and redundancies within the greater periplasmic chaperone network will be necessary to construct a complete mechanistic understanding of gram-negative envelope biogenesis and homeostasis.
